title: A Harvest for the House
premise: Gideon Whitlock, a rationalist property surveyor, arrives at Hollowmere House to appraise it for sale and finds the village's melted church bell ringing each dusk, counting down toward an old debt the house intends to collect. As she maps rooms that rearrange themselves, she uncovers the 1911 story of a servant girl, Edith, betrayed by the family and drowned in the well, whose stolen name was never entered in the parish register. Falling for the last heir, Marlowe, Gideon must choose between her duty to close the sale and her growing conviction that justice, not exorcism, is what the house wants. In the end she registers Edith's name at last, gives up her own claim on the house's future with Marlowe, and walks out as the bell falls silent — though her survey notes now bear a signature not her own.
about_author: Lior Thornbury is the pen name of a former rural land clerk who spent years cataloguing houses no one would buy twice. They write horror from the belief that buildings remember better than people do.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. She arrives at Hollowmere House with instruments, contracts, and a firm disbelief in anything unmeasurable, meeting the reluctant heir Marlowe and his aunts who refuse to leave. The house measures oddly: every room one foot too large. Emotional beat: controlled skepticism beginning to crack at the edges.

chapters.title: A Bell That Was Never Cast
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. At dusk the church bell rings, though the vicar confirms it was melted down in 1911; only Gideon and the household hear it. The aunts begin packing in terror while Marlowe insists they stay. Emotional beat: dread arriving through the most ordinary witness — a surveyor's logbook.

chapters.title: Rooms That Count
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Her measurements reveal a thirteenth room appearing only after dark, cold and smelling of well water. She finds scratch marks inside its walls spelling a woman's name: Edith. Emotional beat: the thrill of evidence curdling into fear of what the evidence wants.

chapters.title: Marlowe's Inheritance
chapters.summary: Marlowe's POV. He confesses his family's shame-kept ledger: wages unpaid, a servant dismissed pregnant in winter 1911, found in the well days later, buried without record. He asks Gideon to finish the sale quickly before the count ends. Emotional beat: guilt passed down like furniture, and first tenderness between them.

chapters.title: The Parish Register
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. In the county archive she discovers Edith Marsh was never entered in any register — legally, she never existed, so no prayer, grave, or justice ever attached to her. The bell has rung eleven times. Emotional beat: righteous anger; Gideon's belief shifts from 'impossible' to 'unjust.'

chapters.title: What the Aunts Know
chapters.summary: Aunt Verity's POV. The eldest aunt recalls childhood games with a maid called Edie and the night her father burned the bell to stop its ringing. She warns Gideon that the house doesn't want them gone — it wants them counted. Emotional beat: complicity across generations, and the cost of silence.

chapters.title: The Well Room
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The thirteenth room opens fully: a stone shaft where the kitchen used to be, water rising with each bell strike. Gideon nearly drowns retrieving Edith's locket; Marlowe pulls her out. Emotional beat: love declared in panic, and the realization that leaving means abandoning Edith forever.

chapters.title: Twelve
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The twelfth bell rings; doors seal, the aunts vanish into the house's shifting corridors, and Marlowe offers himself in his ancestors' place. Gideon refuses both escape and sacrifice, understanding at last what the count demands: a name made official. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: A Harvest for the House
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, climax. She breaks into the sealed parish office at night and enters Edith Marsh into the register — birth, service, death, all witnessed by her own signature. The thirteenth bell rings once, sweetly, and the house exhales; walls settle, water drains, the aunts wake in the garden. Emotional beat: justice outside the law, paid in full.

chapters.title: Signature
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, resolution. The house sells; Marlowe leaves to build a life elsewhere, and their parting is tender but final — she belongs to paperwork and he to freedom. Reviewing her final survey, Gideon finds every measurement exact except one page signed, in faded ink, 'E. Marsh, thanks.' Emotional beat: grief braided with peace; identity shared across a century.
